notes.title: Which rung of the ladder does this task need

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification
The brief says "build an agent". Why are you starting with a workflow?
Tier 2 — Trade-off
What would make you climb to a single agent even though the steps look enumerable?
Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling
You chose a single agent. At 100× the traffic, what breaks first and does the answer change?
Tier 4 — Open-ended design
Design the intake for a system where different requests need different rungs.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The ladder, and the instruction to start at the bottom of it — Building Effective AI Agents (Anthropic)

  • When an agent is warranted vs when a workflow is — the vendor framing of the same fork — A practical guide to building agents (OpenAI, PDF)

  • The token multiple that prices the top rung — How we built our multi-agent research system (Anthropic)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • agentic spectrum — that single call, workflow, agent and multi-agent are four distinct systems, not degrees of the same one.

  • Agents-vs-Workflows — predefined paths versus model-driven control.

  • when-not-build-agent — the cost, latency and reliability case against agency.

What this note adds: the promotion test — the single condition that justifies each step up the ladder, what that step costs in tokens and reliability, and the sentence that wins the point when the interviewer wants you to build the agent anyway.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The four rungs, in order? Single call → workflow → single agent → multi-agent.
What promotes you one rung? Unknown control flow — you can't name the steps ahead of time.
Price of the agent rung? ~4× chat tokens; ~15× at multi-agent (Anthropic).
What makes this question graded? The interviewer is checking you can argue against the thing they asked for.
Strongest reason to stop climbing? The steps are knowable, so a workflow is testable and an agent isn't.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I start at the lowest rung that fits and make the task argue me upward. One model call if the work is a single transformation; a workflow if I can name the steps in advance; a single agent only once the control flow genuinely depends on what comes back mid-task; multi-agent only when the work splits into parts that need separate context windows. Each rung up buys adaptivity and costs tokens, latency and testability. The condition that promotes me is always the same one — I cannot write the steps down before the run starts.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Single model call One transformation — classify, extract, rewrite. Checkable in one shot. Nothing adaptive; a bad input yields a bad output with no recovery. The brief says "given X, produce Y" and never "then, depending on…".
Workflow (fixed graph) You can name every step and branch before the run; the model fills slots. No novel paths — anything unanticipated falls through to an error or a human. The brief reads as a procedure. Stakeholders already drew it as a flowchart.
Single agent (loop + tools) The next step depends on the last result in a way you can't enumerate. ~4× chat tokens, non-deterministic traces, reliability compounding per step. The brief says "figure out" or "investigate", or the search space is unbounded.
Multi-agent Work splits into genuinely parallel parts, or contexts that would poison each other. ~15× chat tokens, coordination failures, errors compounding across handoffs. Sub-tasks are independent and each needs its own large, different context.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Single call Gateway → model → response. No loop, no tool layer, no state store. 1 call. Latency = one prefill + decode. Cost is flat per request. Standard API monitoring. No trace viewer needed.
Workflow A named graph with explicit transitions; each node may call a model. State lives in the graph runner. Steps are known, so cost and p95 are bounded and predictable before launch. You test transitions like code. Failures point at a named node.
Single agent Adds the harness: loop, tool layer, step/token/wall-clock caps, a checkpointer, and a trace span per step. Cost becomes Σ steps, and context is re-billed each step — so it grows roughly with steps². You now need per-step tracing, budget enforcement, and a loop-detection alarm.
Multi-agent Adds an orchestrator, a delegation contract per sub-agent, and shared-state arbitration. ~15× chat tokens. Latency is the slowest branch, not the average. You staff for coordination failures: duplicated work, conflicting writes, lost handoff context.

The diagram test: someone holding this table draws four different box diagrams. If your answer to "why an agent" doesn't add boxes to the picture, you haven't actually promoted a rung — you've just used the word.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

The reliability arithmetic that caps the ladder. Per-step success compounds:

p_task = p_step ^ N

At p_step = 0.95, ten steps gives 0.95^10 ≈ 0.60; twenty gives ≈ 0.36. That is why a workflow with three known steps beats an agent that takes twelve to the same place. (Arithmetic in full; framing in the 95% problem.)

The token multiple that prices the top two rungs. Anthropic's published figures for their research system: an agent uses roughly 4× the tokens of a chat interaction, multi-agent roughly 15×. Say the number out loud when someone proposes five specialist agents for a one-agent task.

The break-even. Promote when the value of adaptivity exceeds the multiple. If a fixed workflow resolves 80% of cases and an agent 92%, the agent buys 12 points of coverage for ~4×. Worth it only when those points are worth more than four calls each. Without coverage numbers, name the measurement: shadow the workflow, count fall-throughs, let that rate decide.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

The questions, in order:

  1. Can I write the steps down before the run starts? Yes → workflow or below. This is the whole fork; the rest is refinement.

  2. Does step N+1 depend on what N returned, in a way I can't branch on in advance? No → it's a long workflow. "Long" is not "agentic".

  3. Do sub-tasks need separate context windows that would poison each other? Only yes reaches multi-agent. "Different roles" does not.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "The classifier works fine in testing but the bill is 20× what we projected, and it's slower than the thing it replaced."

Root cause. A document-triage task built as an agent because the team had just adopted an agent framework. The real work was: extract fields, look up an account, route to one of six queues — every step knowable in advance, a workflow wearing an agent's clothes. With control flow handed to the model, each document ran a variable number of iterations, re-billing accumulated context each time, and sometimes looped on an ambiguous field until the step cap cut it off.

Fix. Rewritten as a fixed graph with the model at two nodes — extraction and disambiguation — and deterministic code elsewhere. Cost returned to projection and p95 became predictable, because step count stopped being a variable. Applying it late cost a framework migration plus an eval re-run, roughly a sprint, all of it avoidable by asking "can I name the steps?" in the first fifteen minutes.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

The brief says "build an agent". Why are you starting with a workflow?

Because "agent" in a brief usually describes the outcome — it should handle the task without a human babysitting it — not the control flow. My job is to find the cheapest structure that produces that outcome, and the cheapest is the one where I own the control flow rather than delegating it.

So I test whether the steps are knowable. If they are, a workflow gives the same user-visible behaviour with bounded cost, a predictable p95, and transitions I can unit-test. If they aren't, I promote — and now I can say exactly why, which is a far stronger answer than having assumed it.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

What would make you climb to a single agent even though the steps look enumerable?

The tell is the shape of the failure cases, not the happy path. If the happy path is three steps but the long tail is fifty different two-step recoveries, enumerating them produces a graph nobody maintains — every new edge case is a code change and a deploy. There the adaptivity is worth the 4×, because the alternative grows without bound.

The second condition is an open-ended search space. "Find the cause" rather than "apply the procedure" means the number of paths isn't large, it's unknown, and a fixed graph can only encode the ones I thought of.

What would not move me: the task being long, being important, or the team wanting to use an agent framework. Long is a workflow with many nodes. Important argues for less non-determinism, not more.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

You chose a single agent. At 100× the traffic, what breaks first and does the answer change?

Cost breaks first, and super-linearly — context is re-billed every step, so spend scales roughly with steps² per run and linearly with runs. The second break is the provider rate limit, which turns into queueing and blows p95 well before compute does.

The answer changes, but not by demoting the whole system. I'd split by case difficulty: run a cheap fixed workflow first and promote to the agent only on fall-through. If 80% resolves in the workflow, the agent's share of volume drops five-fold while keeping the coverage it bought. That hybrid is the usual production shape, and it's only reachable because I know what the workflow rung looks like.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design the intake for a system where different requests need different rungs.

I'd make the rung a routing decision rather than an architectural one, which means the router must be cheap and the rungs must share contracts. A small classifier at the gateway labels each request by control-flow shape — single transformation, known procedure, or open-ended — and that label picks the path.

The rungs then share one tool layer and one state store, so promoting mid-flight doesn't mean re-plumbing: a workflow that falls through emits its partial state as the agent's starting context instead of starting over.

What I'd watch is fall-through rate per label, because it says my routing is wrong. A workflow lane falling through 40% of the time means the classifier under-promotes; an agent lane finishing in three predictable steps means I'm paying the multiple for nothing. Both are readable from the traces the agent rung already needs.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "The task is complex, so it needs an agent."

✅ Reality: Complexity and unknown control flow are different properties. A tax calculation is hugely complex and perfectly enumerable — it wants a workflow. Say "the control flow is unknown ahead of time", not "it's complex".

❌ Trap: "Multi-agent is how you scale an agent."

✅ Reality: Multi-agent parallelises and isolates context. It scales token spend ~15× and multiplies coordination failures. Throughput scaling is worker replicas on the single-agent rung — a deployment concern, not a topology one.

❌ Trap: "Start with the agent, then simplify later if it's too expensive."

✅ Reality: It runs the other way in practice — once control flow lives in the model the steps were never written down, so simplifying means rediscovering them from traces. Promoting on evidence is the cheap direction; demoting is a rewrite.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • agentic spectrum — the four rungs this note makes you choose between.

  • when-not-build-agent — the standing case against the top rungs.

  • the 95% problem — the compounding arithmetic in Section 5.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §1 Autonomy level as a requirement — the rung caps the autonomy: a workflow has no autonomy to set.

  • §1 Metrics before boxes — steps/task and cost/task only go live from the agent rung up.

  • §6 Single vs multi-agent — this note's fourth rung is that decision's entry condition.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Back-office workflow automation — agent vs RPA vs hybrid is this ladder.

  • §14 "Our agent succeeds 60% and costs too much" — the first fix is usually demoting the enumerable parts.

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — the workflow-then-escalate hybrid is the Tier 3 answer here.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • "Find the simplest solution first" — the default the variance question defends — Building Effective AI Agents

  • When an agent is warranted, and the guardrail taxonomy behind the reversibility question — A practical guide to building agents (OpenAI, PDF)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Agents-vs-Workflows — that predefined paths and model-driven control are different systems.

  • Autonomy levels — the assisted → supervised → autonomous ladder.

  • when-not-build-agent — the cost, latency and reliability case against agency.

What this note adds: the five questions in the order that prunes the design space fastest, and the table of what each answer flips in the architecture — the concept notes argue the positions, this one runs the intake.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The five, in order? Variance · verifier · reversibility · latency class · blast radius.
Why variance first? A low-variance answer ends the round early — no agent, no topology debate.
Which answer sets autonomy? Reversibility, per tool and per threshold — never globally.
Which is the HLD set's blind spot? Steps per task; QPS sizes infra, step count sets reliability and cost.
Time budget for intake? ~5 minutes of 45. Past that you're spending architecture time.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

For an agent prompt I run the agentic five, not the standard HLD five. I ask about task variance, whether a verifier exists, whether actions are reversible, the latency class, and the blast radius. Variance goes first because a low-variance answer means no agent at all. Scale questions still get asked — but they size the infrastructure, and for agents the infrastructure is rarely what hurts. What hurts is the loop.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Agentic five (variance, verifier, reversibility, latency, blast radius) The brief contains an action verb — "handles", "resolves", "books", "fixes" ~5 minutes, and you must actually use every answer later "An agent that does X"
Classic HLD five (QPS, data size, read/write mix, latency, consistency) The system is a pipeline with no action loop Under-determines the loop; you'll design infra for a reliability problem "Ingest and serve", "at 50k QPS"
RAG five (corpus, freshness, ACLs, citations, stakes) Retrieval quality is the actual problem Misses agency entirely if the system also acts "Answer questions over our docs"
Agentic five + HLD sizing Agent runs at real volume, or is multi-tenant Longest intake; only worth it when volume genuinely changes the design "4,000 refunds a day across brands"

4. 📐 What It Flips

Answer Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Low variance Fixed workflow; orchestrator is code, not a model One call per step, predictable Ordinary service monitoring
High variance Model-driven loop, tool registry, trace store Steps become a variable you cap Trajectory review, per-run cost alerts
Verifier exists Retry loop closed on the verifier Retries are cheap; budget in steps not reviews Track pass rate per attempt
No verifier Confidence scoring + escalation path Escalation rate × volume = reviewer-hours Staffed review queue, calibration drift
Irreversible actions Approval gate, idempotency keys, compensation path Human latency enters p95 Audit trail, gate-bypass review
Interactive latency Streaming, fewer steps, smaller per-step models Step cap ~5–6 before the budget breaks TTFT and step-latency SLOs
Async latency Queue, checkpoint per step, durable resume Steps cheap, wall-clock budget instead Stuck-run detection, resume tooling
Shared-tenant blast radius Per-tenant isolation, egress allow-list, staged prompt rollout Per-tenant spend caps Injection monitoring on shared sources

The test this table has to pass: someone holding it can redraw the architecture without reopening the concept notes.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

Step count is a reliability decision. End-to-end success is per-step reliability compounded: p^N. At p = 0.95, ten steps lands near 0.60 and twenty near 0.36. Asking "how many steps does a typical task take?" converts a vague reliability worry into a target.

Escalation is a staffing decision. escalation_rate × volume = reviews/day. At 5% of 4,000 refunds/day that is 200 reviews — a rota, not a footnote. The threshold to probe: what review capacity exists today.

Agency is a token multiplier. Anthropic reports agents using roughly 4× the tokens of a chat interaction and multi-agent systems roughly 15× (Building Effective AI Agents). That factor is what "is an agent warranted?" is really weighing.

Intake budget: ~5 minutes of a 45-minute round, two questions minimum. If you can only ask two, ask variance and reversibility — they prune hardest.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

Blast radius isn't a node — it's asked last and scales the answers rather than branching them.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom: a passenger was told by Air Canada's support chatbot that he could claim a bereavement discount retroactively, did so, and was refused — the policy said otherwise.

Root cause: nobody asked who verifies the output, or whether the output was itself a commitment. The bot generated policy statements with no ground-truth check against the policy engine, and a statement to a customer is not reversible.

Fix, applied late: the BC Civil Resolution Tribunal held the airline liable for what its bot said (Moffatt v. Air Canada, February 2024), and the bot was withdrawn. Asked at intake, "is there a verifier?" and "is this output reversible?" would have produced retrieval-with-citation against the live policy plus an abstention path — a design change of days, taken before launch instead of a liability ruling after it.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why not open with QPS and data size like any other design round?

Those size the infrastructure, and for most agents the infrastructure is unremarkable — a few hundred concurrent runs is a small service. They leave the expensive variables untouched.

What varies between two agent systems with identical QPS is steps per task, who decides the next step, and what happens when a step is wrong. Those differences move cost by an order of magnitude and success rate by tens of points, so they get asked first. Sizing questions follow, and only matter to the design when volume pushes the escalation queue or tenant isolation.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

High variance but irreversible actions — which wins?

Neither; the resolution is to split the loop from the effects. Variance argues for a model-driven loop because the paths can't be enumerated in code. Irreversibility argues for tight control because mistakes are permanent. Both hold, and they apply to different halves of the system.

So the agent plans freely over read-only tools — search, fetch, simulate, draft — and every write goes through a narrow set of guarded actions with validated arguments, idempotency keys and an approval gate on the irreversible subset. Latitude over what to propose, none over what executes.

The price is throughput — approvals add human latency — so the next question to ask out loud is what share can run unattended.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

The answers were pinned at 100 tasks/day. What breaks at 100,000?

The approval gate first. A 5% escalation rate is five reviews a day at the small number and 5,000 at the large one, which turns the escalation policy from "when the model is unsure" into a calibrated threshold tuned against reviewer-hours — and that forces confidence calibration to be measured rather than assumed.

Then blast radius stops being hypothetical. At low volume a bad tool call hits one customer and someone notices; at scale, an injected instruction in a shared knowledge source or a bad prompt deploy executes against every tenant within minutes. That is what makes per-tenant spend caps and staged prompt rollout mandatory rather than tidy.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Run a 30-minute requirements session for a team that wants "an AI agent for operations".

Three passes. Inventory first: tasks with volume and current handling time. Vague briefs decompose into four or five concrete tasks with different profiles, and typically half need no model judgment at all.

Second pass scores each task on the five axes. What falls out is a ladder, not a system: reversible, verifiable, high-variance tasks are the genuine agent candidates; irreversible, unverifiable, low-variance ones get a deterministic workflow with a human gate and no agent near them.

Third pass fixes the numbers before any code — task success rate, acceptable escalation rate, cost ceiling per task, p95 completion. That table is the deliverable, and it doubles as the eval plan.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: Asking all five, then designing as if none had been answered.

✅ Reality: Close each loop out loud — "async, so I'll checkpoint per step". Unused answers read as ritual and cost you the credit.

❌ Trap: Treating reversibility as one global property of the system.

✅ Reality: It's per tool and usually per threshold — refunds under $50 auto-approve, above go to a gate. Global answers produce either paralysis or blast radius.

❌ Trap: "The brief says agent, so I'll design an agent."

✅ Reality: Concluding that a workflow suffices is the senior signal. Both Anthropic's and OpenAI's guidance lead with finding the simplest thing that works.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Agents-vs-Workflows — supplies the variance test this intake applies.

  • Autonomy levels — the ladder the reversibility answer selects a rung from.

🔁 Decides / constrains

  • §1 Metrics before boxes — these five answers are what the metrics get set against.

  • §7 Durable execution — the latency-class answer decides whether checkpointing is needed at all.

  • §11 Approval gates — the reversibility answer determines which tools are gated.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — no verifier plus irreversible writes; the intake decides the escalation design.

  • §14 Coding agent — the friendly quadrant; tests as verifier is exactly what this intake surfaces.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Guardrails and human-intervention triggers — the vendor framing of where autonomy stops — A practical guide to building agents (OpenAI, PDF)

  • Permission model and the case for gating actions rather than models — Claude Code: best practices for agentic coding (Anthropic)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Autonomy levels — the assisted → supervised → autonomous ladder and what each rung means.

  • human-in-the-loop — how a gate is implemented once you have decided you need one.

What this note adds: that autonomy is a property of the action, not of the system — the reversibility × cost grid that sets it per tool, and why a single global autonomy setting is the answer that loses the point.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What sets the level? Reversibility × cost of a mistake. Not task difficulty, not ambition.
At what granularity? Per tool, per threshold — never one global setting.
Cheapest way to raise autonomy? Make the action reversible — undo, draft state, soft delete.
Where is the gate enforced? In the tool layer, outside the model. Never in the prompt.
The graded mistake? Setting autonomy from how good the model is, rather than from blast radius.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Autonomy isn't one dial for the system — it's a property of each action, set by how reversible that action is multiplied by what a mistake costs. So I grade tools, not agents. Reading is autonomous, reversible writes are supervised by exception, and anything irreversible and expensive gets a human gate regardless of how good the model is. The lever that actually raises autonomy is engineering reversibility into the action — a draft state or an undo window converts a gated action into an ungated one, which model quality never does.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Assisted — model proposes, human executes Irreversible and expensive: payments, deletions, external comms, anything regulated. Throughput is capped by the human. No overnight or batch operation. The brief names money, customers, or a compliance regime.
Supervised — agent executes, human approves at a gate Reversible but consequential, or irreversible under a threshold value. Latency becomes human-shaped — minutes to days — so the run must be durable. Stakeholders say "we'd want to check it at first".
Autonomous — agent executes, human audits after Reversible, cheap to undo, and high-volume enough that gating would defeat the point. You pay for detection instead of prevention: audit trail, anomaly alerts, rollback tooling. The action has a natural undo, or the blast radius is one record.
Mixed (the real answer) Almost always — different tools in the same agent sit at different rungs. A per-tool policy surface someone must own and keep current as tools are added. The tool list contains both a search call and a refund call.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Assisted No write path from the agent at all. Output lands in a review queue as a proposal. Cheap per run — the loop stops early. Cost moves to human minutes per task. Staff the queue. The metric is reviewer throughput, not agent success rate.
Supervised Adds an approval gate, a durable pause (checkpointer), and a resume-with-payload path. Wall-clock is unbounded; token cost pauses with the run. Escalation rate becomes a live metric. On-call for stuck runs. Approvals need an SLA or the queue silently becomes the bottleneck.
Autonomous No gate, but adds an audit log, anomaly detection, and a rollback/compensation path. Fastest and cheapest per task. Cost shifts into monitoring and the occasional cleanup. You now own incident response for wrong actions taken at machine speed.
Mixed Policy lives in the tool layer: each tool carries its own rung and threshold. Budgets differ per tool — the gated ones dominate p95 while the free ones dominate token spend. Someone owns the policy table, and every new tool needs a rung assigned before it ships.

The redraw test: the gate is a box in the diagram between the loop and the tool layer, and the durable pause is a store. If your answer to "what autonomy level" adds neither, you've set a policy nobody can enforce.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

The grid that settles it. Two axes, four cells — reversibility against cost of a mistake:

Cheap mistake Expensive mistake
Reversible Autonomous Supervised — gate above a threshold
Irreversible Supervised Assisted — human executes

The threshold, where one exists. Gating everything defeats the agent; gating nothing is the incident. So gate on a value threshold and set it from what a wrong action costs to unwind. If a wrong refund costs roughly £40 to reverse in support time and the agent's per-action error rate is ~2%, the expected cost of an ungated action is 0.02 × £40 ≈ £0.80. Gate above the value where that expected loss exceeds the cost of a human glance — if review takes two minutes at £30/hour, that's £1, so actions whose expected loss clears ~£1 get the gate. The inputs are yours to measure; the arithmetic is the part you show.

The measurement to run if you don't have those numbers. Ship supervised with the gate on everything, log every approval decision, and read the approval rate per tool. A tool approved 99% of the time is a candidate for autonomy; a tool approved 60% of the time is telling you the model isn't ready or the tool is too coarse. That log is the evidence that moves a rung, and it's free — you were going to gate at launch anyway.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

You run this per tool, not once. The branch worth saying out loud is the left one: before accepting that an action is irreversible, ask whether it can be made reversible. A send becomes a scheduled send with a cancel window; a delete becomes a soft delete; a write becomes a draft awaiting publish. That engineering move buys more autonomy than any model upgrade.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "It sent the same apology email to a customer four times in ten minutes."

Root cause. The agent had one autonomy setting — autonomous — because the team had reasoned about the agent rather than its tools. Search, ticket lookup and send-email all sat at the same rung. A transient timeout on the mail provider made the send look failed, the loop retried, and because the tool wasn't idempotent and wasn't gated, each retry delivered. The reversibility question had never been asked per tool; it had been answered once, for the whole system, on the basis that the model was accurate.

Fix. Autonomy moved into the tool layer as a per-tool rung, external comms dropped to supervised above a recipient threshold, and the send tool gained an idempotency key so retries collapse. Applying it late cost an apology to the customer, a rushed gate shipped under incident pressure, and a week of trust with the stakeholder who had approved the launch.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

You said supervised. Supervised over what exactly?

Over the actions, not the agent. The agent runs freely — reading, retrieving, reasoning, composing — and the gate sits between the loop and the specific tools whose effects I can't cheaply undo. So a run might make forty autonomous calls and stop once, at the one that matters.

Stating it that way matters because it changes what I build. "The agent is supervised" implies a human watching a run, which doesn't scale and isn't what anyone means. "These three tools require approval above this threshold" is a policy I can implement, test, and hand to whoever owns the tool registry.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

The gate is killing throughput — the approval queue is the bottleneck. What do you change?

First I look at approval rate per tool, because a tool approved 99% of the time is not buying safety, it's buying latency. Those move to autonomous with an audit trail and an anomaly alarm, which catches the rare bad action after the fact at a fraction of the cost.

If the rate is genuinely mixed, I raise the threshold rather than removing the gate — gate the top decile by value and let the rest through, which typically recovers most of the throughput while retaining most of the risk coverage.

The change I'd resist is gating a sample of actions. Sampling works for quality measurement and not for risk, because the damaging action is precisely the one that gets through unsampled.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

At 10× tools, how does the policy stay correct?

It stops being a design artifact and becomes a registry entry with a default of deny. Every tool ships with a rung and a threshold, the default for a new tool is supervised, and promotion to autonomous requires the approval-rate evidence. Without that default, the policy silently decays — someone adds a tool in a hurry and it inherits whatever the framework's default is, which is usually "allowed".

The second thing that breaks is path auditing. With many tools, a gated action can often be reached by an ungated route — a "run script" or "call webhook" tool that reaches the same effect without touching the gated tool. So at scale I'd audit the tool graph for paths that reach an irreversible effect, not just the tools individually. That audit is the part teams skip and the part that produces the incident.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design the approval system for an agent whose runs pause for days.

The gate has to be a durable pause, which makes this a workflow-engine problem rather than a request-handling one. The run checkpoints its full state, emits an approval task with a typed payload — what action, what arguments, what it cost to get here — and the worker releases. Nothing is held in memory, because the approver may act on Monday.

Resume takes the approval as an input to the run rather than a signal to it: the decision, the approver, and a timestamp go into state so the trace explains itself later. That also makes denial a first-class path — the agent needs a branch for "refused", and an agent with no denial branch tends to loop or to find another way to the same effect.

The operational piece people forget is expiry. An approval task with no SLA becomes a silently stuck run, so each gate gets a timeout and a default — usually deny plus escalate — and the queue age is monitored like any other backlog.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "We'll start fully autonomous and add guardrails once we see problems."

✅ Reality: The problems you see first are the cheap ones; the expensive one is the incident you're trying to prevent. Start gated and use the approval log as evidence to remove gates — that direction produces data, the other produces an apology.

❌ Trap: "The model is accurate enough now, so we can raise autonomy."

✅ Reality: Accuracy sets how often you'll be wrong; reversibility and cost set what happens when you are. A 99.9%-accurate agent issuing irreversible payments is still one bad call from an unrecoverable action. Model quality moves the frequency, never the blast radius.

❌ Trap: "Autonomy is set in the system prompt — we tell it to ask before destructive actions."

✅ Reality: That's a request, not a control. Prompt instructions are bypassable by injected content arriving through tool results, and unenforceable when the model simply doesn't follow them. The gate belongs in the tool layer where it's code.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Autonomy levels — the ladder this note assigns per tool.

  • when-not-build-agent — the reversibility argument in its original form.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §4 Read tools vs write tools — this note's per-tool rung is that fork's policy input.

  • §7 HITL as a durable pause — supervised autonomy is what makes durability mandatory.

  • §11 Approval gates on irreversible actions — the same gate, viewed from the security side (permissions and least privilege).

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — refunds are the canonical reversibility × cost cell.

  • §14 Back-office workflow automation — HITL checkpoints are this decision applied per step.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Why consistency across runs, not best-of-k, is the reliability metric for agents — Measuring agent reliability: pass^k (arXiv 2507.10995)

  • Evaluating agents on end-to-end task success rather than component accuracy — A practical guide to building agents (OpenAI, PDF)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Reliability Metrics — pass@k vs pass^k — what the two mean and why they diverge.

  • component vs end-to-end eval — the levels an agent can be measured at.

  • the 95% problem — why per-step accuracy doesn't survive multiplication.

What this note adds: the six-metric commitment made in the first five minutes of a round, what each one forces into the architecture, and why naming them before the boxes is what separates a design from a diagram.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The six? Task success · pass^k · cost/task · steps/task · escalation rate · p95 time-to-complete.
Why before the boxes? Each metric forces a box. Boxes first means instrumenting by accident.
pass@k vs pass^k? @k = any of k succeeds. ^k = all k succeed. Judged on ^k.
Which metric is the cost driver? Steps/task — context is re-billed each step, so cost grows ~steps².
The unit that matters commercially? Cost per successful task, not cost per run.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Before I draw anything I name six numbers: task success rate, pass^k, cost per task, steps per task, escalation rate, and p95 time-to-complete. I do it first because each one forces something into the architecture — pass^k forces verification gates, steps/task forces a step cap, escalation rate forces a human path. If I draw boxes first I end up instrumenting whatever I happened to build. The one I lead with is cost per successful task, because it's the only number that gets worse when reliability drops, and it's the one finance eventually asks about.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Task success rate leads The task has a checkable definition of done and the business cares about coverage. Says nothing about consistency — a 90% agent may be 90% on different 10% each run. The brief has a verifier: tests, schema, SQL results.
pass^k leads The same input will be run repeatedly and users notice variance more than failure. Brutal numbers early; k=5 at 90% per-run is 59%, which reads as regression to stakeholders. The brief says "reliable", "consistent", or the output feeds an automated downstream.
Cost per successful task leads Volume is high and margin is the constraint. Optimising it pushes toward fewer steps and smaller models, which can cap achievable quality. Someone in the room owns a budget, or the word "per-seat" appears.
p95 time-to-complete leads The agent is interactive or sits in a user-facing flow. Forces step reduction and parallelism early, before you know which steps mattered. The brief names a latency class, or a human is waiting.

4. 📐 What It Flips

Metric Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Task success rate Needs a definition of done that code can evaluate — a verifier box, or a labelled eval set. Eval runs become a recurring cost line, not a one-off. A regression gate in CI on every prompt, tool, model or graph change.
pass^k Forces verification gates and retry-with-check, because consistency can't be prompted into existence. Re-running k times per eval multiplies eval cost by k. You report a distribution, not a number. Variance becomes an on-call signal.
Cost per task Forces token attribution per step, a spend cap in the gateway, and usually a model router. Makes context growth visible — the steps² term stops being invisible. Per-tenant spend caps and a cost dashboard someone reads weekly.
Steps per task Forces a step cap and loop detection into the harness. Directly sets both cost and latency; it is the lever both others hang off. Step-count distribution is the first thing you look at when either regresses.
Escalation rate Forces a human path to exist at all — queue, SLA, resume-with-payload. Human minutes become a real line item. Staff the queue; a rising rate is either model drift or scope creep.
p95 time-to-complete Forces streaming, parallel tool calls, and a wall-clock budget. Trades cost for latency — parallelism raises token spend. p95 not mean, because the tail is where the timeouts and the abandons live.

The redraw test: five of these six add a box or a cap to the diagram. If you can name a metric and nothing changes in the picture, you named a KPI, not a design constraint.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

pass^k is the one that surprises people. If a single run succeeds with probability p, then all of k independent runs succeeding is:

pass^k = p ^ k

At p = 0.90, pass^5 = 0.90^5 ≈ 0.59. So an agent everyone calls "90% reliable" delivers a consistent result across five attempts about three-fifths of the time. That gap is why the arXiv work above argues consistency is the metric that matters for deployment — best-of-k flatters an agent that a user experiences as flaky.

Cost per successful task, which is the commercial number.

cost_per_success = cost_per_run / task_success_rate

A run costing £0.30 at a 60% success rate is £0.50 per success, not £0.30 — and improving success from 60% to 80% cuts the real unit cost to £0.375 without touching token spend at all. That is the argument for spending on verification rather than on a cheaper model, and it is the single most useful piece of arithmetic to have ready in a cost conversation.

Steps per task, the lever underneath both. Because the accumulated context is re-billed on every step, run cost grows roughly with the square of step count while latency grows linearly. Halving steps from twelve to six therefore cuts cost by roughly 4× and latency by about 2× — which is why "reduce steps" is the first optimisation, ahead of model routing and caching.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

The questions, in order:

  1. Is there a verifier? It decides whether your lead metric can be automatic (task success) or has to be human-derived (escalation rate, edit rate). This is the same fork as §1's verifier note, which is why the two get asked together.

  2. Who is waiting? A human waiting makes p95 a hard budget rather than a report. Nobody waiting turns latency into a cost question instead.

  3. What is the cap for each? A metric without a number is a wish. "Task success above 85%, under 8 steps, under £0.40 per success, p95 under 30 seconds" is a design constraint you can be held to — and it's what makes the rest of the round concrete.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "The demo was flawless and the pilot users say it's unreliable."

Root cause. The team had measured task success on a fixed eval set and hit 88%, which everyone treated as the reliability number. What they had never measured was consistency: the same request run twice often took different paths and produced different results, because nothing in the harness constrained the trajectory. Users didn't experience 88% success — they experienced the same question answered differently on Tuesday, which reads as broken rather than as statistically fine. The metric set had no pass^k in it, so the variance was invisible until humans met it.

Fix. Added pass^k at k=3 to the eval, which came back near 55% and explained the complaints immediately. The remedies were verification gates on the two steps with the highest branch factor and a lower temperature for the planning step. Adding it late cost the pilot's credibility and a re-run of the whole eval suite, when the metric could have been committed to in the first five minutes of design.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

Why name metrics before the architecture? Isn't that backwards?

It's the opposite of backwards — the metrics are what make the architecture fall out. If I commit to pass^k, verification gates are no longer optional. If I commit to a p95, a step cap and streaming are decided. Naming them first means the boxes have reasons, and every box I draw can be traced to a number I promised.

Doing it the other way produces a diagram that looks complete and instruments whatever happens to be easy. That's how teams end up with detailed token dashboards and no idea what their task success rate is.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

You can only have three of the six. Which, and what do you give up?

Task success, steps per task, and escalation rate. Success is the definition of working; steps is the lever that sets both cost and latency, so it's a proxy for two of the others; escalation rate is the honest signal when there's no verifier and also the thing that costs real money in people.

What I give up is pass^k and p95 as first-class numbers, which means I'd be blind to variance and to the tail. That's tolerable for a batch agent and not tolerable for an interactive one, so in an interactive brief I'd swap escalation rate out for p95 and accept the blindness on the human side instead.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

At 100× volume, which of these stops being measurable the way you defined it?

pass^k, because you can't re-run production traffic k times — it's an offline metric and offline sets go stale. At scale I'd keep pass^k on a fixed regression set in CI and add an online proxy: variance in output length or in step count for structurally identical requests. A widening distribution is usually consistency degrading before task success moves.

Cost per successful task also gets harder, because "successful" needs a label and labels are the scarce thing at volume. The practical substitute is the escalation and human-edit signal — treat an escalated or edited run as a failure and you get a continuously updating denominator for free, at the price of a slightly pessimistic number.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design the measurement layer for an agent platform serving many teams.

The platform owns the metric definitions and the teams own the thresholds, because the failure mode in a shared platform is every team inventing its own definition of "success" and no number being comparable. So the tracing layer emits a fixed schema — a span per step with tokens, cost, tool name, outcome — and success is a per-team predicate evaluated over the final state rather than something each team logs by hand.

That gives cost per successful task, steps per task and p95 for free from the same trace, which matters because getting teams to instrument voluntarily doesn't work. pass^k runs in CI against each team's eval set, gated on prompt, tool, model or graph changes.

The part I'd design carefully is attribution. With shared tools and a shared model router, cost has to be attributable to a tenant and a feature or the platform can't charge back and nobody optimises. That means a tenant tag propagated through every span, which is a plumbing decision best made before the first team onboards rather than retrofitted across twenty.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "We measure accuracy per step — it's 97%, so we're in good shape."

✅ Reality: Per-step accuracy multiplies. At 97% over fifteen steps, end-to-end is 0.97^15 ≈ 0.63. Step accuracy is a debugging metric; the number you commit to is end-to-end task success.

❌ Trap: "Cost per run is our unit economic."

✅ Reality: Failed runs cost money and deliver nothing, so the unit is cost per successful task. It's the version that improves when you add a verifier, which is exactly the investment cost-per-run makes look pointless.

❌ Trap: "We'll use pass@k — it's the standard agent benchmark metric."

✅ Reality: pass@k rewards best-of-k, which matches a benchmark leaderboard and not a production user who gets one run. Deployment reliability is pass^k, and the two diverge fast: at p=0.9, k=5, it's 0.99 versus 0.59.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Reliability Metrics — pass@k vs pass^k — the definitions this note commits to.

  • the 95% problem — the multiplication behind the step-accuracy trap.

  • tracing & observability — the layer every one of these numbers is read from.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §8 Hard budgets — steps/task and p95 are where the step cap and wall-clock cap get their values.

  • §12 Layered eval — the metric set decides which eval levels you actually need to build.

  • §10 Unit economics — cost per successful task is this note's number, carried into the cost section.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 "Our agent succeeds 60% and costs too much" — the whole problem is stated in two of these six metrics.

  • §14 Coding agent — tests as verifier make task success automatic, which is why it's the easy case.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Tests and execution as the checkable signal an agent loops against — SWE-bench: can language models resolve real-world GitHub issues? (arXiv 2310.06770)

  • Why a critic without a ground truth is weaker than a deterministic check — Building Effective AI Agents (Anthropic)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • component vs end-to-end eval — the levels an agent's output can be judged at.

  • llm-as-judge for trajectories — how a model-based critic works and where it's unreliable.

What this note adds: that the presence or absence of a cheap ground-truth check is a single fact that reshapes the whole architecture, and the substitute you build when the honest answer is "there isn't one".

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What counts as a verifier? A cheap, deterministic check the agent can run mid-loop: tests, schema, SQL, compile.
What it buys architecturally? A self-correction loop — the agent can retry against a signal instead of guessing.
What replaces it when absent? Confidence-based escalation to a human; the human becomes the verifier.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

The first thing I check is whether a cheap, deterministic verifier exists — tests that run, a schema that validates, a query that returns rows. If one does, the architecture gets a self-correction loop and success becomes measurable automatically. If one doesn't, I stop trying to manufacture confidence inside the model and design for escalation instead: the agent produces a draft with a confidence signal, and a human is the verification step. Almost every expensive agentic mistake I've seen comes from pretending a critic model is a verifier when nothing grounds it.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Strong verifier — tests, compiler, schema, SQL result The domain produces a machine-checkable artifact. Verification time per iteration, and a sandbox to run it in. The brief mentions code, queries, structured output, or a spec.
Weak verifier — rules, heuristics, constraint checks Output is partly checkable: required fields present, totals reconcile, citations resolve. Catches format errors and misses semantic ones, which is the failure people trust it not to have. The output has structure but the content is judgement.
Critic model — LLM-as-judge in the loop Nothing deterministic exists and you need some signal before a human sees it. Doubles cost per iteration for a correlated opinion — the judge shares the generator's blind spots. Free-text output: summaries, advice, research.
No verifier — escalate Output is judgement and being wrong is consequential. Human minutes per task, and a queue with an SLA to staff. Support, medical, legal, anything where "plausible but wrong" is the risk.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Strong verifier Self-correction loop: act → verify → retry. Needs a sandbox and a bounded retry count. More steps per task, but each retry is productive — cost buys measured progress. Task success is automatic, so CI regression gates come nearly free.
Weak verifier A validation gate before the write, not a loop. Failures route to human, not to retry. Cheap — the check is code. You must monitor what it misses; false confidence is its whole risk.
Critic model An extra model call per iteration, plus a cap so critic and generator can't ping-pong. Roughly doubles per-iteration cost for an unverifiable gain. Judge drift is now a thing you monitor. Rubric changes need their own eval.
No verifier No loop at all past the first draft. Adds confidence scoring, an escalation path, a review queue and a resume path. Cost moves from tokens to human minutes; escalation rate becomes the headline metric. Staff and SLA the queue. The queue, not the model, is your bottleneck.

The redraw test: a strong verifier puts a cycle in the diagram; no verifier puts a human box and a queue in it. If the answer changes nothing in the picture, you haven't answered it.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "The agent is confidently wrong about a quarter of the time, and we have no way to tell which quarter."

Root cause. A research-summarisation agent was built with a critic model as its quality gate, on the assumption that a second model reading the output was equivalent to a check. It isn't — the critic was the same model family reading the same retrieved context, so it inherited the generator's misreadings and approved them. There was no ground truth anywhere in the loop, so the "verified" label meant only that two correlated models agreed.

Fix. The critic was demoted from gate to hint, and the real check became citation resolution — every claim had to map to a retrieved span, which is deterministic and cheap. Claims that didn't resolve were stripped and the run escalated. That converted an unmeasurable system into one with a hard signal, but only after the wrong-answer rate had been discovered by the users rather than by the eval.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • llm-as-judge for trajectories — why a critic is a weak substitute here.

  • trajectory evaluation — judging the path — judging the path when the output can't be judged.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §1 Metrics before boxes — a verifier makes task success automatic; without one the lead metric becomes escalation rate.

  • §8 Verification gates — this note decides whether that section has anything deterministic to gate on.

  • §3 Reflection / critic loops — worth it only when the critique can be checked, which is this fork.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Coding agent — tests are the verifier; this is the easy end of the fork.

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — no verifier, so confidence-based escalation is the design.

  • §14 Deep research agent — citation resolution is the closest thing to a verifier available.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The MICRO preset this note paces against — ai_design_prompt_v4.md

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • the architects framing — what the round is actually grading.

What this note adds: the clock — where the minutes go in an agent prompt specifically, and the two places they get lost.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Intake budget? ~5 minutes. Past that you're spending architecture time.
When is the ladder argument due? Minute 5–10, before any boxes. It's graded.
Where do rounds get lost? Over-clarifying, and drawing the loop before naming the metrics.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

An agent prompt isn't paced like a standard HLD round — the scaling maths isn't what's graded, the control-flow argument is. Five minutes intake, five arguing which rung of the ladder the task needs, ten on architecture and tool contracts, ten on reliability and cost with real numbers, and ten held back for the failure questions, which is where the round is won. Capacity estimation gets a sentence, not a slide.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
MICRO pacing (45 min, one agent) Standard agent prompt — "design a support agent that can issue refunds". No room for a deep multi-agent topology debate; you name it and move on. One system, one user journey, one set of tools.
MACRO pacing (60+ min, platform) "Design an internal agent platform for many teams" — tenancy, registry, shared eval. Less depth per component; you're sketching seams, not tool schemas. The brief names multiple teams, tenants, or an ecosystem.

Pick the preset before drawing — the two spend their middle twenty minutes on different things.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • the architects framing — what's being graded, which is what the clock serves.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §1 Clarifying questions — the five-minute intake cap is what forces that note's ordering.
